Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) -- Afghan lawmakers have directly accused Pakistan's intelligence agency of involvement in a string of deadly attacks in Afghanistan, blasting their neighbor as "the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism." The recent attack by a suicide bomber on the Indian embassy in Kabul killed more than 40 people. A Pakistani official Tuesday bristled at the accusation, saying that Afghan lawmakers were making allegations without proof. "We are not an irresponsible nation and we don't blame our failures on others," said a senior official with Pakistan's Directorate for Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI). "If they want to engage in this kind of game, let them be." The Afghan Cabinet made the scathing indictment in a resolution Monday, saying Afghanistan would boycott a series of meetings with Pakistan unless "bilateral trust" is restored. In recent weeks a wave of attacks carried out by Islamic militants have killed scores of people in Afghanistan, including an assault on a military outpost Sunday that killed nine U.S. soldiers, as well as a suicide attack on the Indian Embassy a week ago that killed 58 people. The two incidents, along with an assassination attempt against Afghan President Hamid Karzai at a military ceremony on April 27, are "indicative of the attempts by the ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence) to once again occupy Afghanistan and to perish the true right of the people of Afghanistan for national sovereignty," the resolution said. Afghanistan regularly accuses Pakistan's intelligence service -- which once had strong ties with the Taliban -- of orchestrating attacks inside its borders. Pakistan has repeatedly denied involvement, including in the incidents that the resolution cited. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates also said there is no indication that "foreign agents" were responsible for the embassy attack. The senior ISI official said Tuesday that if Afghanistan has proof that Pakistani intelligence agents were involved in the attacks, that proof should be presented and the ISI will act on it. The official said that the Pakistani government could also blame incidents in Pakistan, like recent attacks in Karachi and Hangu, on others. But without proof, he said, it would be irresponsible. Pakistan and Afghanistan have a tumultuous history that dates back several years. During the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, religious schools in Pakistan helped train fighters who battled the Soviets. After the Taliban took over Afghanistan in 1996 and imposed fundamentalist rule, Pakistan was one of the few countries that recognized the regime diplomatically. It dropped its support after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in Washington and New York. But Afghanistan claims that Pakistan continues to informally support the militants, who operate from havens in Pakistan's lawless tribal regions near the porous 1,500-mile border the two countries share. Adding fresh ammunition to the suspicions, the Rand Corp. -- a U.S. think tank -- released a report last month that said some members of Pakistan's intelligence service and its paramilitary corps were helping insurgents in Afghanistan. The study, funded by the U.S. Defense Department, alleged that members of the two agencies often tipped off militants to the location and movement of coalition forces trying to rout them. It also said personnel within the agencies trained fighters at camps in Pakistan, financed them and helped them cross the border into Afghanistan. The Pakistani military denied and denounced the report, calling it a "smear campaign" designed to "create doubts and suspicion in the minds of (the) target audience." Relations between the two countries are strained to such a point that Karzai has threatened to send troops across the border to take on the militants. "The people of Afghanistan and the international community have come to the reality that Pakistan intelligence institutions and its army have become the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism and extremism to the world and particularly to Afghanistan," Monday's resolution said.

outputs.L1:
KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) -- Afghan lawmakers have directly accused Pakistan's intelligence agency of complicity in a series of deadly attacks across Afghanistan, denouncing their neighbor as "the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism." The recent suicide bombing at the Indian embassy in Kabul claimed more than 40 lives.

A senior Pakistani official reacted sharply to the accusation on Tuesday, asserting that Afghan lawmakers were leveling allegations without substantiating evidence. "We are not an irresponsible nation, and we do not blame our failures on others," said the official from Pakistan's Directorate for Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI). "If they wish to engage in this kind of game, let them proceed."

The Afghan Cabinet issued its scathing condemnation in a resolution passed Monday, declaring that Afghanistan would boycott a series of scheduled meetings with Pakistan until "bilateral trust" is restored. In recent weeks, a wave of attacks by Islamic militants has claimed numerous lives in Afghanistan, including an assault on a military outpost Sunday that killed nine U.S. soldiers, and a suicide attack on the Indian Embassy a week earlier that left 58 people dead.

According to the resolution, these two incidents—along with an assassination attempt against Afghan President Hamid Karzai during a military ceremony on April 27—are "indicative of the attempts by the ISI to once again occupy Afghanistan and to extinguish the true right of the Afghan people to national sovereignty."

Afghanistan has long accused Pakistan's intelligence service, which once maintained close ties with the Taliban, of orchestrating attacks within its borders. Pakistan has consistently denied any involvement, including in the incidents cited in the resolution. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates likewise stated there is no evidence indicating that "foreign agents" were responsible for the embassy attack.

The senior ISI official said Tuesday that if Afghanistan possesses proof implicating Pakistani intelligence agents in these attacks, such evidence should be presented, and the ISI would act accordingly. He noted that the Pakistani government could similarly attribute domestic incidents—such as recent attacks in Karachi and Hangu—to external actors, but doing so without proof would be irresponsible.

Pakistan and Afghanistan share a turbulent history spanning several decades. During the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, religious schools in Pakistan helped train fighters who resisted Soviet forces. After the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan in 1996 and imposed fundamentalist rule, Pakistan was among the few nations to diplomatically recognize the regime—support it withdrew following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in Washington and New York.

Afghanistan nonetheless maintains that Pakistan continues to informally support militants operating from safe havens in its lawless tribal regions along the porous 1,500-mile border shared by the two countries. Lending further credence to these suspicions, the RAND Corporation—a U.S. think tank—released a report last month asserting that certain members of Pakistan's intelligence service and paramilitary corps have been aiding insurgents in Afghanistan.

The study, commissioned by the U.S. Defense Department, alleged that personnel within these two agencies frequently alerted militants to the location and movements of coalition forces attempting to root them out. It further claimed that agency personnel trained fighters at camps in Pakistan, provided them with financial support, and facilitated their crossing into Afghanistan. The Pakistani military rejected and condemned the report, characterizing it as a "smear campaign" intended to "create doubts and suspicion in the minds of [the] target audience."

Relations between the two nations have deteriorated to such a degree that President Karzai has threatened to deploy troops across the border to confront the militants directly.

"The people of Afghanistan and the international community have come to realize that Pakistan's intelligence institutions and its army have become the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism and extremism to the world, and particularly to Afghanistan," Monday's resolution stated.

# Escalating Tensions: Afghanistan Accuses Pakistan's ISI of Terror Sponsorship

A significant diplomatic rift has emerged between Afghanistan and Pakistan, as Afghan lawmakers have leveled serious accusations against Pakistan's premier intelligence agency, the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI). In pointed remarks that reflect deepening frustration with cross-border security threats, Afghan officials have directly implicated the ISI in orchestrating a series of deadly attacks within Afghanistan's borders. The rhetoric employed has been notably harsh, with lawmakers characterizing Pakistan as "the largest center for breeding and exporting terrorism"—language that underscores the severity of the diplomatic breakdown between the two neighboring nations.

## Pakistan's Firm Rebuttal

Pakistani officials have not remained silent in the face of these allegations. A senior ISI official issued a firm rejection of the Afghan claims, characterizing them as unsubstantiated accusations lacking credible evidence. The official pushed back forcefully against the narrative being advanced by Afghan lawmakers, emphasizing that Pakistan does not engage in the practice of deflecting blame for its own internal security failures onto other nations. This response reflects Islamabad's broader position that it has consistently been unfairly scapegoated for instability that originates from complex, multifaceted security challenges within Afghanistan itself.

## Formal Diplomatic Action

The dispute escalated beyond mere rhetorical exchanges when the Afghan Cabinet took concrete diplomatic action. The Cabinet passed a formal resolution stating that Afghanistan would boycott upcoming bilateral meetings with Pakistan until what officials termed "bilateral trust" could be restored between the two countries. This move represents a significant escalation, transforming verbal accusations into official government policy and signaling that Kabul intends to leverage diplomatic isolation as a means of pressuring Islamabad to address its concerns.

## Evidence Cited in the Resolution

The Afghan Cabinet's resolution was not issued in a vacuum; it specifically cited several high-profile violent incidents as evidence supporting claims of ISI involvement in destabilizing Afghanistan. Among the incidents referenced were:

- **The Indian Embassy attack**: A devastating suicide bombing targeting the Indian Embassy in Kabul that claimed 58 lives, representing one of the deadliest attacks against a diplomatic mission in the country.

- **The assault on a military outpost**: An attack on a military installation that resulted in the deaths of nine U.S. soldiers, highlighting the direct threat posed to coalition forces operating in the region.

- **The assassination attempt on President Karzai**: An attempt on the life of Afghan President Hamid Karzai, which Afghan officials viewed as a direct challenge to the nation's leadership and sovereignty.

Afghan lawmakers presented these incidents collectively as part of a pattern suggesting deliberate ISI efforts to destabilize the Afghan government and undermine the country's sovereignty.

## Contradicting International Assessment

Adding a complex dimension to this diplomatic dispute, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates offered an assessment that appeared to contradict key elements of the Afghan resolution. Regarding the Indian Embassy attack specifically, Gates stated that there was no indication that "foreign agents" were responsible for the bombing. This assessment from a key international stakeholder and security partner complicates the narrative being advanced by Afghan officials, suggesting that the available evidence may not fully support the direct ISI involvement being alleged, at least in the case of the embassy attack.

This divergence between Afghan accusations and American intelligence assessments highlights the challenges in definitively establishing responsibility for such attacks, while also illustrating the broader complexities facing international efforts to stabilize Afghanistan amid ongoing regional tensions and competing narratives about the sources of continued violence.

# The Enduring Story of Kabul: Afghanistan's Capital in Global Focus

Kabul, the capital city of Afghanistan, has remained a focal point of international attention for decades, with news organizations like CNN providing continuous coverage of the events shaping this historic city and nation. Nestled in a valley surrounded by the Hindu Kush mountains, Kabul has witnessed profound transformations throughout its long history as a crossroads of trade, culture, and conflict along the ancient Silk Road.

In recent decades, Kabul has become synonymous with major geopolitical events that have captured global attention. CNN and other international news outlets have reported extensively on the city through periods of war, political upheaval, and attempts at rebuilding. The Taliban's return to power in August 2021 marked one of the most significant moments in the city's modern history, as international forces withdrew after two decades of military presence, and images of chaotic scenes at Kabul's airport were broadcast worldwide.

Throughout these turbulent periods, journalists have worked to document the human stories behind the headlines—the experiences of Afghan civilians, families separated by conflict, women navigating dramatically changing social conditions, and the international community's evolving relationship with Afghanistan. CNN's correspondents have often provided on-the-ground reporting from Kabul, offering viewers insights into daily life amid political instability, humanitarian challenges, and the resilience of the Afghan people.

Beyond the headlines of conflict, Kabul remains home to millions of residents navigating everyday life—markets bustling with commerce, schools attempting to provide education, and communities striving for normalcy despite ongoing challenges. The city's cultural heritage, including historic sites and traditions, continues to exist alongside contemporary struggles.

International media coverage of Kabul serves multiple purposes: informing global audiences about developments affecting regional and international security, highlighting humanitarian needs, and preserving a historical record of a pivotal period in Afghan history. As Afghanistan continues to navigate its complex political and social landscape, Kabul remains central to understanding the broader narrative of the nation's past, present, and uncertain future.

The relationship between global journalism and events in places like Kabul underscores the vital role that international reporting plays in fostering understanding across cultures and borders, even as it raises ongoing questions about representation, context, and the complexities of conveying nuanced realities to global audiences.

counterfactuals.output:
# Afghan Lawmakers Accuse Pakistan's ISI of Orchestrating Deadly Attacks

*By CNN Staff*

**KABUL, Afghanistan** — Tensions between Kabul and Islamabad escalated sharply this week after several members of Afghanistan's parliament publicly accused Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) agency of orchestrating a string of recent terrorist attacks on Afghan soil, reigniting decades-old accusations that have long strained relations between the neighboring countries.

The claims came during a heated parliamentary session in Kabul, where lawmakers presented what they described as intelligence gathered by Afghan security services linking recent bombings to networks allegedly supported by Pakistani intelligence operatives.

"We have credible information showing coordination between certain elements within the ISI and militant groups operating across our border," one senior lawmaker told reporters following the session. "This is not the first time, and unless the international community holds Pakistan accountable, it will not be the last."

## Background of Longstanding Distrust

The accusations tap into a deep well of mistrust between the two nations. Afghan officials have for years alleged that elements within Pakistan's security establishment maintain ties to militant networks, including factions of the Taliban and other armed groups, as a means of exerting influence over Afghanistan's internal affairs.

Islamabad has consistently denied these allegations, characterizing them as attempts by Kabul to deflect blame for internal security failures.

"These accusations are baseless and unhelpful," a spokesperson for Pakistan's Foreign Ministry said in a statement Wednesday. "Pakistan has been a victim of terrorism itself and continues to support regional stability. We categorically reject any insinuation of state involvement in attacks against Afghan civilians."

## Renewed Scrutiny Amid Regional Instability

The latest accusations come at a particularly volatile moment, with Afghanistan continuing to grapple with attacks attributed to various militant factions, including ISIS-Khorasan (ISIS-K) and splinter groups. Analysts note that pinpointing responsibility in the country's complex security landscape remains notoriously difficult, complicating efforts to verify claims made by either side.

"There's a long history of both genuine security cooperation failures and politically motivated accusations in this relationship," said one regional security analyst who has studied Afghan-Pakistani relations for over a decade. "Separating verified intelligence from political rhetoric is extremely challenging, especially in public forums like parliament."

The analyst noted that similar accusations have surfaced periodically since the early 2000s, often coinciding with periods of heightened diplomatic tension or domestic political pressure within Afghanistan.

## International Response

The international community has largely urged restraint from both sides. A spokesperson for the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) called for "credible, transparent investigations" into any attacks before attributing responsibility, while emphasizing the importance of regional cooperation in combating terrorism.

Officials from Washington, who have historically walked a delicate line in relations with both Kabul and Islamabad, have not issued a formal response to the latest allegations but have previously acknowledged concerns about militant safe havens along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.

## What Comes Next

It remains unclear whether Afghan authorities will present formal evidence to international bodies or pursue the matter diplomatically. Pakistani officials have called for any accusations to go through "appropriate diplomatic channels" rather than public political forums.

Meanwhile, residents in Afghan border regions—who have borne the brunt of recurring violence—say they are less concerned with the diplomatic finger-pointing than with concrete action to prevent further attacks.

"We hear these accusations every few months," said one shopkeeper in Kandahar. "What we want is safety, not more words."

CNN has reached out to Pakistan's ISI for comment but has not received a response as of publication.

---

*This story is developing and will be updated.*

# Afghanistan-Pakistan Relations Deteriorate Following Deadly Suicide Attacks

## A Fragile Border Relationship Reaches New Lows

Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have plummeted to their lowest point in recent years following a series of suicide bombings that have claimed dozens of lives and reignited decades-old tensions between the two neighboring nations. The attacks, which officials on both sides have attributed to different militant networks, have triggered a diplomatic crisis marked by accusations, troop movements, and the temporary closure of key border crossings.

## The Attacks and Their Immediate Aftermath

The most recent wave of violence began when a series of coordinated suicide bombings struck civilian and military targets in both countries within a span of several weeks. In Afghanistan, attacks in Kabul and provincial capitals killed scores of civilians and security personnel, while similar bombings in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and Balochistan resulted in significant casualties among both military and civilian populations.

Afghan officials were quick to point fingers across the border. "These attacks are being planned and launched from safe havens inside Pakistani territory," said an Afghan Interior Ministry spokesperson. "We have provided evidence to Pakistani authorities on multiple occasions, yet the networks responsible continue to operate with impunity just kilometers from our shared border."

Pakistani officials have firmly rejected these characterizations, instead redirecting blame toward Afghan soil. "It is Pakistan that has suffered the most from terrorism emanating from Afghan territory," stated a spokesperson for Pakistan's Foreign Ministry. "Groups hostile to Pakistan have found sanctuary in Afghanistan, and despite repeated requests, the Afghan authorities have failed to take decisive action against these elements."

## Diplomatic Fallout

The exchange of accusations has moved beyond rhetoric into concrete diplomatic action. Pakistan's Foreign Office summoned the Afghan chargé d'affaires to lodge a formal protest, presenting what officials described as "credible intelligence" linking recent attacks to militants operating from Afghan provinces bordering Pakistan.

"We have shared specific coordinates and intelligence regarding training camps," a senior Pakistani security official told reporters on condition of anonymity. "The patience of the Pakistani people and government is not limitless. We expect concrete action, not just condemnation."

Kabul's response was equally forceful. Afghanistan's Foreign Ministry issued a statement rejecting what it called "baseless allegations" and countered that Pakistan should look inward. "Instead of leveling accusations against Afghanistan, Pakistan should address the terrorist infrastructure that has existed on its own soil for decades," the statement read. "Afghanistan has been a victim of terrorism for over four decades, much of it exported from beyond our borders."

## Border Closures and Economic Impact

In the wake of the attacks, Pakistan temporarily closed the Torkham and Chaman border crossings—vital arteries for trade and the movement of people between the two countries. The closures, ostensibly implemented for security reasons, have had immediate economic repercussions, stranding thousands of trucks carrying perishable goods and disrupting supply chains that both economies depend upon.

Afghan traders have voiced frustration over the economic toll. "Every day the border remains closed costs us millions in losses," said one trader's association representative in Kandahar. "We are being punished for something we had no part in. Ordinary people and businesses are paying the price for a political and security dispute."

Pakistani officials have defended the closures as necessary precautions. "Border security is paramount right now," explained a spokesperson for Pakistan's Interior Ministry. "We cannot allow the free movement of individuals across the border when we have credible threats of further attacks being planned."

## Military Posturing

Adding to the tension, both nations have reported increased military activity along their shared 2,600-kilometer border, one of the most volatile frontiers in the region. Pakistani military sources confirmed conducting airstrikes on what they described as "terrorist hideouts" within Afghan territory, a claim that drew sharp condemnation from Kabul.

"This is a flagrant violation of Afghanistan's sovereignty," declared a statement from Afghanistan's Ministry of Defense. "Pakistan cannot use the pretext of counter-terrorism to conduct unilateral military operations inside our country. We reserve the right to respond to any future violation of our airspace or territory."

Pakistani military officials defended the strikes as legitimate self-defense measures. "When our own territory and citizens are threatened by elements operating from across the border, we have both the right and responsibility to act," a military spokesperson said during a press briefing in Islamabad. "These were precision operations targeting specific militant infrastructure, not attacks against the Afghan state or its people."

## Regional and International Reactions

The escalating tensions have drawn concern from regional powers and international observers who fear a broader destabilization of an already fragile region. Diplomatic sources indicate that neighboring countries, including China and Iran, have quietly urged both sides to exercise restraint and pursue dialogue rather than unilateral action.

Analysts note that the current crisis reflects deeper, structural issues that have plagued the bilateral relationship for years, including disputes over the Durand Line border, the presence of various militant groups on both sides, and competing regional interests involving other global and regional powers.

"This is not simply about the recent attacks," explained one regional security analyst. "This is about a fundamentally broken trust between two governments that have long accused each other of harboring and supporting proxies. Until there is a genuine mechanism for intelligence sharing and joint counter-terrorism cooperation, these cycles of violence and recrimination will continue."

## Civilian Toll and Humanitarian Concerns
